title: You Were Told to Love God—So Why Does the Bible Tell You to Fear Him?
paragraphs: You Were Told to Love God—So Why Does the Bible Tell You to Fear Him?
Understanding “The Fear of the Lord” Correctly—and why losing it may explain why we can sing about a holy God on Sunday while casually negotiating with sin on Monday.
There is a kind of fear that makes you run away.
And there is a kind of fear that finally makes you fall to your knees.
Confuse the two, and you can misunderstand one of the most important truths in Scripture.
Maybe you have heard the phrase your whole life:
“The fear of the Lord.”
And perhaps, somewhere deep inside, you never quite knew what to do with it.
Are Christians supposed to be terrified of God?
Are we supposed to approach Him expecting punishment at any moment?
If God is our Father, why should His children fear Him?
If “God is love” (1 John 4:8), why does Scripture repeatedly command people to fear Him?
And if 1 John 4:18 says that “perfect love casts out fear,” why does Proverbs tell us that fear is where wisdom begins?
Those questions matter because two opposite errors can quietly deform our understanding of God.
One turns God into a cruel tyrant from whom we desperately try to escape.
The other turns Him into a harmless grandfather whose holiness, commands, and judgment can safely be ignored.
Neither picture is biblical.
The God revealed in Scripture is infinitely loving—and unimaginably holy.
He welcomes sinners.
But He never becomes comfortable with sin.
He is Father to those who belong to Christ.
But He does not stop being King.
He is gracious.
But grace never means that God has surrendered His throne.
And perhaps this is where the fear of the Lord begins to make sense.
Proverbs 1:7 opens the door with words that have echoed across thousands of years:
יִרְאַת יְהוָה רֵאשִׁית דָּעַת
Yir’at YHWH re’shit da‘at.
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.”

The Hebrew expression יִרְאַת יְהוָה — yir’at YHWH means, quite literally, “the fear of Yahweh.” The noun yir’ah comes from the Hebrew root yare’, a word whose biblical range can include actual fear or dread, but also awe, reverence, and profound respect. In Proverbs, the expression is not describing the irrational terror of someone hiding from an unpredictable monster. It describes a creature rightly responding to the overwhelming holiness, authority, greatness, and moral perfection of the Creator. The NET translators note that the expression can hold together both shrinking back before God's awesome majesty and drawing near in reverence and adoration.
That distinction changes everything.
The fear of the Lord is not pretending God is less frightening by making Him smaller.
It is seeing God as He actually is.
Holy.
Sovereign.
Good.
Judge.
Father.
Creator.
Redeemer.
The One before whom angels worship.
The One who knows the thought you never spoke aloud.
The One who sees what happens after the browser history is erased.
The One who heard what you said when nobody from church was listening.
The One who knows whether your worship is surrender or performance.
And still...
the One who sent His Son for sinners.
This is where the subject becomes uncomfortable.
Because many of us are not actually afraid that God will abandon us.
We have become afraid that He might interrupt us.
We want Jesus as Savior without Jesus interfering too deeply with our private lives.
We want forgiveness without repentance.
Comfort without correction.
Heaven without holiness.
A cross that removes guilt without a King who challenges our idols.
We may say, “God knows my heart,” while forgetting that this is one of the most sobering truths imaginable.
Yes.
He does.
He knows all of it.
That hidden resentment.
That secret relationship.
That private addiction.
That dishonest transaction.
That bitterness you have renamed “boundaries.”
That pride you call “discernment.”
That envy you disguised as criticism.
That lust you keep promising to quit.
That compromise nobody else knows exists.
And the fear of the Lord begins when the reality of God becomes greater to you than the approval, pleasure, money, relationship, ambition, or secret sin sitting in front of you.
This is why Proverbs does not leave “fear” floating as an abstract religious emotion.
It becomes behavior.
“The fear of the LORD is hatred of evil” (Proverbs 8:13).
That is devastatingly practical.
You can sing beautifully and still not fear God.
You can quote Scripture and still not fear God.

You can have Christian merchandise, Christian playlists, Christian friends, Christian vocabulary, and a Christian-looking social media profile while quietly making peace with what Christ died to save you from.
The fear of God is revealed when obedience costs something.
Joseph understood something like this when temptation entered a private room.
Potiphar's wife offered him something his flesh could have rationalized.
Nobody needed to know.
No congregation was watching.
No accountability partner was standing nearby.
Yet Joseph's deepest objection was not merely, “I might get caught.”
It was:
“How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?” (Genesis 39:9).
There it is.
God was more real to Joseph in the secret room than the temptation standing in front of him.
That is fear of the Lord.
Not merely being frightened by consequences.
Being captured by the reality of God.
And Scripture gives us an extraordinary picture of this tension at Sinai.
The people encounter thunder, lightning, smoke, trumpet blast, and a trembling mountain. They recoil.
Then Moses says something that initially sounds almost contradictory:
“Do not fear,” and yet God has come so “the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin” (Exodus 20:20).
Do not fear...
so that you may fear.
That sentence alone destroys the shallow idea that every biblical use of “fear” means exactly the same psychological experience.

There is a terror that drives people from God, and there is a holy fear that awakens them to who God is and restrains them from treating evil casually. The linguistic and contextual evidence surrounding the Hebrew expression supports this tension rather than reducing yir’ah to only one English synonym.
Think about standing near the edge of an enormous cliff overlooking the ocean.
You may be overwhelmed by its beauty.
You may want to stay there.
But if you understand reality, you do not casually dance backward with your eyes closed.
Beauty and danger are not contradictions.
Awe changes how you move.
How much more when standing before the living God?
Biblical fear does not mean believing God is evil.
It means knowing He isn't ordinary.
And this is something our generation desperately needs to recover.
We have sometimes made God so approachable in our imagination that He has become manageable.
But the God of Scripture cannot be domesticated.
Isaiah saw the Lord “high and lifted up,” and his first response was not, “I feel empowered.”
He cried:
“Woe is me!”
Peter witnessed Christ's miraculous power and said:
“Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.”
John—the disciple who had reclined near Jesus at supper—later encountered the glorified Christ and fell at His feet “as though dead.”
Familiarity with Jesus never gave the apostles permission to trivialize His glory.
And then comes the breathtaking part.
Jesus touches John.
“Fear not.”
Do you see it?
Holiness brought him down.
Grace came near.
That is the Gospel.
Christianity does not solve the terrifying holiness of God by pretending He was never holy.
The Gospel reveals how sinful people can be reconciled to this holy God without God compromising His righteousness.
And the answer is Jesus Christ.
At the cross, something infinitely greater than motivational religion happened.
Sin was not waved away as though it did not matter.
Our rebellion was not dismissed with a sentimental shrug.
Christ bore sin.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
The cross therefore tells you two things simultaneously.
Your sin is more serious than you wanted to believe.
And God's mercy is greater than you dared to hope.
Look at Jesus bleeding beneath the weight of human sin and you will never again be able to say that sin doesn't matter.
Look at Jesus willingly giving Himself for sinners and you will never again be able to say that mercy isn't available.
Calvary destroys both arrogance and despair.
And that helps us understand another verse people sometimes place against the fear of the Lord:
“There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment” (1 John 4:18).
John is speaking in the context of confidence regarding judgment. The believer's hope is not that judgment ceased to exist, but that our confidence rests in God's love manifested in Christ.
The Christian therefore does not need to live every morning wondering whether God is itching to condemn those who are in Christ.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
But freedom from condemnation does not produce casualness toward holiness.
It should produce deeper worship.
Imagine a guilty prisoner legitimately sentenced to death.
Then imagine the door opening.
Someone enters.
Someone innocent.
Someone says:
“I will take his place.”
The prisoner walks free.
Would the appropriate response be:
“Wonderful. Now I can commit more crimes”?
Paul anticipated almost exactly that distortion of grace:
“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?”
His answer is explosive:
“By no means!”
Grace is not permission to return comfortably to the chains Jesus broke.
Grace changes what freedom means.
That is why the fear of the Lord and the love of God are not enemies.
Healthy biblical fear says:
God is so holy that I dare not treat sin lightly.
The Gospel says:
God is so loving that Christ died to rescue me from it.
And discipleship says:
Because He loved me like that, I no longer want the darkness that was killing me.
This is not salvation by good behavior.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works that allow us to boast (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But do not stop reading before verse 10.
The people saved by grace are recreated in Christ for good works.
Grace does not merely change our destination.
Grace begins changing us.
Maybe that is why this article feels more personal than you expected.
Maybe there is something you have been negotiating with.
Something you keep calling “a struggle” even though somewhere inside you know you have begun protecting it.
There is a difference between fighting sin and furnishing a room for it.
A believer may stumble.
A believer may fall terribly.
Peter did.
David did.
The Bible is brutally honest about human failure.
But the mark of grace is not sinless perfection.
It is that Christ keeps calling us out of hiding.
Repentance means we stop defending what God is trying to deliver us from.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Come into the light.
Not because Jesus is waiting with folded arms to humiliate you.
Because He already knows.
And He is still calling.
Remember Peter.
He denied Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
The rooster crowed.
Peter realized what he had done.
And he wept.
Imagine those tears.
The man who had promised loyalty now had to live with the memory of his own voice saying, in effect:
I don't know Him.
What do you do when your greatest spiritual scandal becomes something you cannot undo?
Jesus shows us.
After the resurrection, Christ did not pretend Peter's failure never happened.
He met him.
Restored him.
Recommissioned him.
“Do you love me?”
Peter's scandal did not get the final sentence.
Jesus did.
That is what grace does.
Grace does not rewrite history by calling evil good.
Jesus rewrites the future by redeeming people who could never repair their past by themselves.
From scandal...
to grace.
Maybe that is your story too.
Or maybe it needs to become your story tonight.
The fear of the Lord is not God shouting, “Stay away from Me.”
For the person being drawn to repentance, it is the devastating realization:
“I cannot keep treating the God who gave everything for me as though He deserves whatever pieces of my life I happen to have left.”
It is realizing that Jesus is not an accessory to your life.
He is Lord.
And perhaps the most dangerous spiritual condition is not trembling before God.
Perhaps it is reaching the point where nothing about God makes us tremble anymore.
When sin no longer grieves us.
When Scripture can no longer correct us.
When conviction is immediately labeled judgment.
When repentance sounds offensive.
When holiness sounds extreme.
When Jesus becomes inspirational but no longer authoritative.
That is not freedom.
That is spiritual anesthesia.
Proverbs tells us that the fear of the LORD is the רֵאשִׁית — re’shit of knowledge—the beginning, starting point, foundation from which wisdom grows.
Wisdom begins when God gets His proper place.
Not you.
Not culture.
Not your feelings.
Not me.
God.
That means sometimes Scripture will confront something we desperately want to keep.
And at that moment the question becomes painfully simple:
Who is Lord?
Jesus once told His disciples not to fear those who can kill the body and then can do nothing more, but to recognize God's ultimate authority (Luke 12:4–5).
The New Testament uses the language of φόβος — phobos, “fear,” and the related verb φοβέομαι — phobeomai, which can carry meanings involving fear, reverence, or respect according to context.
The New Testament did not simply erase the fear of God after the resurrection.
Acts 9:31 describes the church as “walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit.”
Notice those companions.
Fear of the Lord.
Comfort of the Holy Spirit.
Not enemies.
Together.
Reverence without grace becomes crushing.
Grace without reverence becomes cheap.
But biblical Christianity gives us the holy God who brings sinners near through the blood of Christ and then teaches His redeemed people to walk differently because they belong to Him.
So perhaps we need to stop asking:
“Should Christians be afraid of God?”
and ask the better question:
“What kind of fear does the Gospel remove, and what kind does grace deepen?”
Christ delivers His people from slavish terror of condemnation.
Yet knowing Christ should deepen our reverence, humility, worship, obedience, and astonishment before God.
You do not fear Him because He is evil.
You fear Him because He is God.
And when that truth finally moves from theology into your bones, ordinary decisions begin changing.
What you watch changes.
What you hide changes.
How you speak to your spouse changes.
How you conduct business changes.
What you do with money changes.
How you behave when nobody is watching changes.
How quickly you repent changes.
Because suddenly the question is no longer merely:
“Can I get away with this?”
It becomes:
“How could I willingly cherish what grieves the One who loved me enough to go to the cross?”
That is where fear begins turning into worship.
And maybe right now you know exactly what God has put His finger on.
Don't bury it beneath another video.
Don't numb it with another distraction.
Bring it to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive mercy.
Walk forward.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only person struggling toward the light.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
It protects you from things pretending to be joy while quietly destroying you.
Not as a religious performance. Not as a way of earning God's favor. Christ alone saves, by grace through faith.

But if this ministry is helping people encounter Scripture, repentance, hope, and Jesus, then supporting and sharing that work can be one practical way of participating in its mission. Send this to the friend who has confused grace with permission.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting God Himself.
God does not need our money.
We need His mercy.
He is glorified when hearts trust His Son, repent of sin, worship Him, obey His Word, love others, pursue holiness, proclaim the Gospel, and steward what He has given them for His purposes.
That distinction matters.
Because the fear of the Lord will not allow us to manipulate people in God's name.
It makes us tremble at the thought of doing so.
And perhaps that is the final test.
The fear of the Lord is not primarily demonstrated by how loudly we say God's name.
It is demonstrated by how seriously we take Him when nobody is applauding.
So tonight...
when the screen goes dark...
when the crowd disappears...
when the temptation returns...
when nobody would ever know...
remember Joseph.
Remember Peter.
Remember Sinai.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember the cross.
Remember the blood.
Remember that the One you fear is also the One who loved sinners enough to be pierced for them.
And remember this:
The fear of the Lord does not make grace smaller—it makes you finally understand how astonishing grace really is.
